summary: Defines a profile of TLS and DTLS versions 1.2 and 1.3 for use with the US Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) Suite. It sets which capabilities and configuration choices are used by US National Security Systems, and is also appropriate for other US Government systems that handle high-value information. It is published openly for developers and operators.

plainLanguage.summary: Government computers follow a strict recipe of locks and keys for private chats. This note publishes that recipe so makers can follow it.

questions: what is cnsa suite for tls
which tls cipher suites does nsa require
subtitle: NSA's recipe for secure TLS and DTLS configuration using approved algorithms.

tldr.problem: Different organizations may implement TLS in incompatible ways, and not all algorithm choices are suitable for protecting highly sensitive government communications.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies exactly which TLS and DTLS versions, cipher suites, algorithms, and configuration options must be used by US National Security Systems to ensure strong cryptography and interoperability.
tldr.outcome: NSA-operated systems follow a consistent security profile, and developers building systems for government use can confidently implement compatible security.

today: RFC 9151 remains the current NSA profile for CNSA-compliant TLS and DTLS implementations in US National Security Systems.

sections.title: What This Profile Covers
sections.content:
The National Security Agency (NSA) has published a profile of TLS (Transport Layer Security) and DTLS (Datagram Transport Layer Security) protocols for use in US National Security Systems. Instead of defining new protocols, this RFC narrows down the options that TLS and DTLS allow.

The profile applies to all four protocol versions: TLS 1.2, TLS 1.3, DTLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.3. It specifies which cipher suites, algorithms, curves, and configuration options MUST be used. The profile is publicly available so that developers and operators building systems for government or high-value information can implement it.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a checklist saying: when you set up a secure connection for government, use these exact locks and these exact keys, not others.

sections.title: The CNSA Suite
sections.content:
The Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite (CNSA) is a set of cryptographic algorithms approved by NSA. The Suite reflects the prospect of quantum computers, which may break today's cryptography, so CNSA provides a transition path that avoids requiring two major algorithm changes in a short timeframe.

CNSA approves the following for TLS: AES-256-GCM for encryption, SHA-384 for hashing, ECDSA with the NIST P-384 curve for digital signatures, and RSA with 3072-bit or 4096-bit keys. For key establishment, CNSA allows ECDH (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman), DH (Diffie-Hellman), or RSA key transport, depending on the TLS version.
sections.plainLanguage: CNSA is a list of approved locks (encryption), seals (signatures), and key-making methods that are strong and will stay safe for a long time.

sections.title: TLS and DTLS Configuration Requirements
sections.content:
For TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2, clients MUST offer at least one of four approved cipher suites: TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, or TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384. The CNSA cipher suites MUST be the first (most preferred) choices offered in the ClientHello message.

For TLS 1.3 and DTLS 1.3, the client MUST offer the single cipher suite TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 as the first preference, and MUST include supported groups for ECDHE secp384r1, DHE ffdhe3072, or DHE ffdhe4096 for key agreement.

The RFC also specifies requirements for signature algorithms, the extended master secret extension (for TLS 1.2), session resumption, certificate validation, and certificate revocation checking via CRL or OCSP.
sections.plainLanguage: When asking for a secure connection, always list the approved government locks first. Use these exact versions of the encryption and signature methods, and always check that the other side's ID card is real.

sections.title: Certificates and Key Material
sections.content:
Certificates used in CNSA TLS/DTLS connections MUST be signed with ECDSA or RSA and MUST comply with the CNSA Suite Certificate and CRL Profile (RFC 8603). Both the TLS 1.2 and 1.3 specifications require that the server authenticate to the client; the server MAY also authenticate the client as needed by the application.

For RSA signatures in TLS 1.2, the profile requires support for RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 and recommends RSASSA-PSS. For TLS 1.3, RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 is required for certificates, but RSASSA-PSS is required for handshake message signatures. RSA moduli MUST be either 3072 bits or 4096 bits. The RSA exponent MUST satisfy the constraint 2^16 < e < 2^256 and be odd.
sections.plainLanguage: The ID cards (certificates) must be signed with one of the approved signature methods. The bigger the RSA key, the safer the signature.

sections.title: Security Notes
sections.content:
The profile forbids TLS versions prior to 1.2, as they are weaker. Implementations MUST NOT use elliptic curves, RSA schemes, or finite fields outside those defined in the profile, as using weaker algorithms would compromise the security of the entire cipher suite.

TLS 1.3 forbids the early_data extension because early data does not have replay protection, which is a security risk. Session resumption in TLS 1.3 MUST use Ephemeral ECDHE or DHE with SHA-384 key derivation.
sections.plainLanguage: Never use old versions of TLS—they have security holes. Never mix approved and non-approved locks. Some fancy TLS features are turned off because they are risky.

sections.title: Status
sections.content: RFC 9151 is an Informational RFC published in April 2022. It has not been obsoleted and remains the current NSA profile for CNSA-compliant TLS and DTLS implementations in US National Security Systems and other US Government systems processing high-value information.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the official rulebook, and it is still the rulebook today.
